learningObjectives.title: Mechanisms, the rate-determining step and intermediates
Reading the energy profile of a multistep reaction
Order of reaction and its graphs
The rate constant and its units
The Arrhenius equation and its straight-line form
The Arrhenius factor, and finding Ea and A from data

questions.q: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen: 2NO(g) + 2H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Which proposed mechanism is consistent with both the rate equation and the overall equation?
options: 2NO → N₂O₂ (slow); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂; H₂O₂ + H₂ → 2H₂O (both fast)
2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂ (slow); H₂O₂ → 2OH (fast)
2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O as a single step, in one collision of all four molecules
2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O (slow); N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O (fast)
optionWhy: A student who assumes the first step is rate-determining picks this. The steps add up correctly to the overall equation, but with a slow first step the rate equation would be rate = k[NO]², with no H₂ term, which does not match the data.

A student who checks only the rate equation picks this. The slow step, after the fast first step, gives rate = k[NO]²[H₂], but the steps add up to 2NO + H₂ → N₂ + 2OH, not the overall equation, so the mechanism is inconsistent with the stoichiometry.

A student who reads the overall equation as one collision picks this. A simultaneous collision of four molecules is extremely unlikely, and a single step would give rate = k[NO]²[H₂]², not the observed rate equation.

The steps add up to 2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O once the intermediates N₂O₂ and N₂O cancel. The slow second step involves N₂O₂ (formed from 2NO in the fast first step) and H₂, so the rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Here the rate-determining step is not the first step.
questions.explain: The steps add up to 2NO + 2H₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O once the intermediates N₂O₂ and N₂O cancel. The slow second step involves N₂O₂ (formed from 2NO in the fast first step) and H₂, so the rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Here the rate-determining step is not the first step.

questions.q: Nitrogen dioxide reacts with carbon monoxide: NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g), ΔH = −226 kJ mol⁻¹. The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[NO₂]². The proposed mechanism is step 1: 2NO₂(g) → NO₃(g) + NO(g); step 2: NO₃(g) + CO(g) → NO₂(g) + CO₂(g). Which statement about the energy profile for this mechanism follows from these data?
options: The first maximum is the highest point on the profile, as step 1 is the rate-determining step.
The rise from the reactants to the first maximum exceeds that from the minimum to the second, as step 1 is slow.
NO₃ and NO sit at the top of the first maximum, as they are the species formed in step 1.
The first maximum is the transition state of a unimolecular step, as only NO₂ reacts in step 1.
optionWhy: A student who measures every activation energy from the original reactants concludes that the rate-determining step must have the highest maximum. Step 2 starts from the intermediate, so its activation energy is the rise from the minimum; if the intermediate lies well above the reactants, the second maximum can be the higher point even though step 2 has the smaller activation energy. The data fix only which rise is larger.

The rate equation contains NO₂ to the second power, matching the two NO₂ molecules that collide in step 1, and does not contain CO, which reacts only in step 2; so step 1 is the rate-determining step. The rate-determining step is the step with the largest activation energy, so the rise from the reactants to the first transition state is larger than the rise from the intermediate (NO₃ + NO, with CO) to the second. The profile has two maxima, a minimum for the intermediate, and ends 226 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants.

A student who treats a transition state as a real species, like an intermediate, places NO₃ and NO at the first maximum. NO₃ is the intermediate: it is formed in step 1 and used in step 2, so it sits in the minimum between the two maxima. The first maximum is a transition state, with bonds partly broken and partly formed, which cannot be isolated.

A student who counts kinds of reactant particle calls step 1 unimolecular because only NO₂ reacts. Two NO₂ molecules collide in step 1, so it is bimolecular, which is also why the rate equation is second order with respect to NO₂.
questions.explain: The rate equation contains NO₂ to the second power, matching the two NO₂ molecules that collide in step 1, and does not contain CO, which reacts only in step 2; so step 1 is the rate-determining step. The rate-determining step is the step with the largest activation energy, so the rise from the reactants to the first transition state is larger than the rise from the intermediate (NO₃ + NO, with CO) to the second. The profile has two maxima, a minimum for the intermediate, and ends 226 kJ mol⁻¹ below the reactants.

questions.q: A proposed mechanism for the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g) is: step 1: I₂(g) ⇌ 2I(g) (fast); step 2: H₂(g) + 2I(g) → 2HI(g) (slow). Which statement about molecularity in this mechanism is correct?
options: Step 2 is bimolecular, as it involves two different reacting species, H₂ and I.
The slow step is termolecular, as one H₂ molecule and two I atoms must all collide together in it.
Step 1 is termolecular, as three particles, one I₂ molecule and two I atoms, appear in it.
The overall reaction is bimolecular, as one H₂ molecule collides with one I₂ molecule.
optionWhy: A student who counts the kinds of species picks this. Molecularity counts particles, not kinds: the coefficient 2 means two I atoms take part alongside one H₂ molecule, so three particles collide and the step is termolecular.

Molecularity is the number of reacting particles in an elementary step. In step 2 three particles, one H₂ molecule and two I atoms, react in one collision, so the step is termolecular. A simultaneous three-particle collision with the correct orientation is improbable, which is consistent with step 2 being the slow step.
A student who counts the products as well as the reactants picks this. Only the reacting particles count: a single I₂ molecule breaks apart in step 1, so the forward step is unimolecular.

A student who reads the overall equation as a single collision picks this. Molecularity applies only to elementary steps; the overall equation gives the stoichiometry, and in the proposed mechanism H₂ never collides with I₂ but with two I atoms.
questions.explain: Molecularity is the number of reacting particles in an elementary step. In step 2 three particles, one H₂ molecule and two I atoms, react in one collision, so the step is termolecular. A simultaneous three-particle collision with the correct orientation is improbable, which is consistent with step 2 being the slow step.

questions.q: The initial rate of the reaction A + 2B → C was measured at constant temperature. Experiment 1: [A] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.060 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the rate equation?
options: rate = k[A]¹[B]²
rate = k[A]⁴[B]³
rate = k[A]¹[B]¹
rate = k[A]²[B]¹
optionWhy: A student who takes the orders from the coefficients in A + 2B → C picks this. The data show the rate quadruples when [A] doubles (second order in A) and triples when [B] triples (first order in B).
A student who takes the order as the factor by which the rate changes picks this. The order is the exponent: 2ⁿ = 4 gives n = 2 for A, and 3ⁿ = 3 gives n = 1 for B.
A student who assumes the rate is directly proportional to every concentration picks this. Doubling [A] quadruples the rate, so the order in A is 2, not 1.

Experiments 1 and 2: [A] doubles with [B] constant and the rate increases by 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4 = 2², so the order in A is 2. Experiments 2 and 3: [B] triples with [A] constant and the rate increases by 18 ÷ 6.0 = 3 = 3¹, so the order in B is 1.
questions.explain: Experiments 1 and 2: [A] doubles with [B] constant and the rate increases by 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4 = 2², so the order in A is 2. Experiments 2 and 3: [B] triples with [A] constant and the rate increases by 18 ÷ 6.0 = 3 = 3¹, so the order in B is 1.
questions.working: Exp 1 → 2: [A] × 2, [B] constant, rate × (6.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 4 = 2², so order in A = 2. Exp 2 → 3: [B] × 3, [A] constant, rate × (1.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(6.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 3 = 3¹, so order in B = 1. Rate = k[A]²[B]; overall order 3.

questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². At constant temperature, the concentrations of A and B are both doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
optionWhy: A student who adds the separate effects gets 2 + 4 = 6. The concentration terms in the rate equation are multiplied, so the factors multiply: 2 × 4 = 8.
A student who takes the overall order as the factor by which the rate changes gets 3. The overall order is an exponent: doubling every concentration multiplies the rate by 2³ = 8.

The factors multiply: doubling [A] (first order) multiplies the rate by 2¹ = 2, and doubling [B] (second order) multiplies it by 2² = 4, so the rate increases by 2 × 4 = 8, which is 2 raised to the overall order, 3.
A student who treats each reactant as first order gets 2 × 2 = 4. B is second order, so doubling [B] alone quadruples the rate; the total factor is 2 × 4 = 8.
questions.explain: The factors multiply: doubling [A] (first order) multiplies the rate by 2¹ = 2, and doubling [B] (second order) multiplies it by 2² = 4, so the rate increases by 2 × 4 = 8, which is 2 raised to the overall order, 3.

questions.q: The graph shows how the initial rate of the reaction A + B → C varies with the initial concentration of A, with [B] and the temperature kept constant. Which statement is correct?
options: The order with respect to A is zero, so [A] does not appear in the rate equation, although A is consumed.
A takes no part in the reaction, since changing its concentration has no effect on the rate.
A graph of [A] against time for this reaction would also be a horizontal line, as the rate does not depend on [A].
The order with respect to A is one, since doubling [A] multiplies the rate by a factor of one.
optionWhy: A horizontal rate–concentration graph means the rate is independent of [A]: the order with respect to A is zero, so [A]⁰ = 1 and A is omitted from the rate equation, rate = k[B]ⁿ. A is still a reactant and is used up as the reaction proceeds.

A student who thinks a zero-order reactant does not react picks this. A is consumed, as the equation shows; it is zero order because it is not involved in the rate-determining step, so its concentration does not affect how fast the reaction goes.

A student who carries the shape of the rate–concentration graph over to the concentration–time graph picks this. Because the rate is constant, [A] falls at a constant rate: the [A]–time graph is a straight line with a negative gradient, not a horizontal line.

A student who takes the order to be the factor by which the rate changes picks this. Order is the exponent of [A] in the rate equation: doubling [A] leaves the rate unchanged, which means 2ⁿ = 1 and n = 0. For first order the rate would double.
questions.explain: A horizontal rate–concentration graph means the rate is independent of [A]: the order with respect to A is zero, so [A]⁰ = 1 and A is omitted from the rate equation, rate = k[B]ⁿ. A is still a reactant and is used up as the reaction proceeds.

questions.q: The graph shows how the concentration of A changes with time for the reaction 2A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction is second order with respect to A, as the coefficient of A in the equation is 2.
The reaction is zero order with respect to A, as A is being used up at one steady rate.
A graph of rate against [A] for this reaction would be a curve of the same shape, falling to zero.
The reaction is first order with respect to A, as [A] halves in equal time intervals.
optionWhy: A student who takes orders from the coefficients of the balanced equation picks this. Orders can only be found experimentally, from data such as this graph. The constant half-life of 50 s shows first order; for second order the half-life would double each time the concentration halved.

A student who assumes a reaction proceeds at one steady rate picks this. The graph is a curve, not a straight line: [A] falls by 0.040 in the first 50 s but only by 0.020 in the next 50 s, so the rate falls as [A] falls. A zero-order reactant would give a straight line.

A student who carries the concentration–time shape over to the rate–concentration graph picks this. The constant half-life shows first order, rate = k[A], so a graph of rate against [A] is a straight line through the origin, rising as [A] increases.

The concentration falls from 0.080 to 0.040, to 0.020 and to 0.010 mol dm⁻³ in equal 50 s intervals: a constant half-life. A constant half-life, independent of the starting concentration, is the signature of a first-order reaction, rate = k[A].
questions.explain: The concentration falls from 0.080 to 0.040, to 0.020 and to 0.010 mol dm⁻³ in equal 50 s intervals: a constant half-life. A constant half-life, independent of the starting concentration, is the signature of a first-order reaction, rate = k[A].

questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]²[B]. When [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³, the rate is 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the value of k?
options: 0.030 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
1.5 × 10⁻² mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
6.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who treats A as first order divides by [A][B] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ and gets 0.030. The rate equation has [A]², so divide by (0.020)² × 0.050 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵.
A student who calculates [A]² as 2 × [A] divides by 2 × 0.020 × 0.050 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ and gets 1.5 × 10⁻². (0.020)² = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴, so k = 1.5.
A student who multiplies instead of dividing gets 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. k = rate/([A]²[B]) = 1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.
questions.working: k = rate/([A]²[B]) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/((0.020 mol dm⁻³)² × 0.050 mol dm⁻³) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol³ dm⁻⁹) = 1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

questions.q: A plot of ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis, in K⁻¹) for a reaction is a straight line with a gradient of −6.00 × 10³ K. Using ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the activation energy of the reaction?
options: 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹
6.00 × 10³ J mol⁻¹
0.722 kJ mol⁻¹
4.99 × 10⁴ kJ mol⁻¹
optionWhy: The gradient is −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R = 6.00 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹. The negative gradient shows that k increases as T increases.

A student who takes the gradient as −Ea, leaving out R, gets Ea = 6.00 × 10³ J mol⁻¹. That number is Ea/R, in K; the gradient is −Ea/R, so multiply by R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to obtain Ea = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who divides by R when rearranging gets 6.00 × 10³ ÷ 8.31 = 722, read as 722 J mol⁻¹ = 0.722 kJ mol⁻¹. From gradient = −Ea/R, multiplying both sides by −R gives Ea = −gradient × R = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
A student who reads the result of 6.00 × 10³ × 8.31 as kJ mol⁻¹ gets 4.99 × 10⁴ kJ mol⁻¹. With R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ the result is in J mol⁻¹: 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: The gradient is −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R = 6.00 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹. The negative gradient shows that k increases as T increases.
questions.working: ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A has the form y = mx + c, so gradient = −Ea/R. Ea = −gradient × R = −(−6.00 × 10³ K) × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: The graph shows ln k plotted against 1/T for a reaction; two points on the line are marked. Using ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the activation energy of the reaction?
options: 8.0 kJ mol⁻¹
66 kJ mol⁻¹
0.96 kJ mol⁻¹
0.066 kJ mol⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who takes the gradient as −Ea, leaving out R, reads 8.0 × 10³ as Ea in J mol⁻¹ and writes 8.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The gradient is −Ea/R, so Ea = 8.0 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 66 kJ mol⁻¹.

Between the marked points ln k falls by 8.0 while 1/T rises by 1.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so the gradient is −8.0 × 10³ K. The gradient equals −Ea/R, so Ea = 8.0 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 6.65 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ≈ 66 kJ mol⁻¹.
A student who divides the gradient by R gets 8.0 × 10³ ÷ 8.31 = 963 J mol⁻¹ = 0.96 kJ mol⁻¹. Rearranging gradient = −Ea/R by multiplying both sides by −R gives Ea = −gradient × R = 66 kJ mol⁻¹.

A student who ignores the 10⁻³ in the axis label takes Δ(1/T) as 1.0 K⁻¹, giving a gradient of −8.0 K and Ea = 8.0 × 8.31 = 66 J mol⁻¹ = 0.066 kJ mol⁻¹. The axis numbers are 1/T in units of 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so Δ(1/T) = 1.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, the gradient is −8.0 × 10³ K and Ea = 66 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: Between the marked points ln k falls by 8.0 while 1/T rises by 1.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so the gradient is −8.0 × 10³ K. The gradient equals −Ea/R, so Ea = 8.0 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 6.65 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ≈ 66 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.working: Reading the marked points: (1/T = 2.5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −2.0) and (1/T = 3.5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −10.0). Gradient = Δ(ln k)/Δ(1/T) = (−10.0 − (−2.0)) ÷ ((3.5 − 2.5) × 10⁻³ K⁻¹) = −8.0 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = −8.0 × 10³ K. Since gradient = −Ea/R, Ea = −gradient × R = 8.0 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 6.65 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 66 kJ mol⁻¹ (2 s.f.).

questions.q: Reaction 1 occurs between two gaseous atoms. Reaction 2 occurs between two large gaseous molecules and happens only if they collide at one particular site on each molecule. Assume the two reactions have the same Ea and the same collision frequency at a given temperature. Which reaction has the larger Arrhenius factor, A, and why?
options: Reaction 1, as a greater fraction of its collisions have a suitable orientation for reaction.
Neither: A depends only on the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, which is the same.
Neither: A depends only on how often the particles collide, which is the same for both.
Reaction 2, as A is larger when collisions must have one particular orientation to react.
optionWhy: A takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations. Atoms can react whichever way they meet, but the large molecules react only when their reactive sites meet, so a smaller fraction of their collisions are properly oriented and A is smaller for reaction 2.

A student who confuses A with the energy term picks this. The fraction with E ≥ Ea is e^(−Ea/RT), which is indeed the same here; A describes the frequency of properly oriented collisions, which differs.
A student who ignores collision geometry picks this. A counts collisions with proper orientations, not all collisions; most collisions between the large molecules miss the reactive site.

A student who reads 'A takes orientation into account' as 'A is bigger when orientation matters more' picks this. A counts only the collisions that are properly oriented, so the strict orientation requirement of reaction 2 makes its A smaller, not larger.
questions.explain: A takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations. Atoms can react whichever way they meet, but the large molecules react only when their reactive sites meet, so a smaller fraction of their collisions are properly oriented and A is smaller for reaction 2.

questions.q:
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)   K = 50 at temperature T
A sealed vessel at temperature T contains H₂, I₂ and HI, each at a concentration of 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Which statement describes what happens as the mixture reaches equilibrium at temperature T?
options: There is net backward reaction, and [HI] decreases.
No net reaction occurs, as the concentrations are equal.
There is net forward reaction, and [HI] increases.
K becomes 1.0, and the concentrations stay the same.
optionWhy: A student who has the Q–K rule the wrong way round picks this. Q = 1.0 is less than K = 50, so more product is needed and the net reaction goes forward.
A student who thinks equilibrium means equal concentrations picks this. Equal concentrations give Q = 1.0, not K = 50, so the mixture is not at equilibrium.
Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 0.20²/(0.20 × 0.20) = 1.0. Q < K, so the ratio of product to reactant terms is too small: net forward reaction increases [HI] and decreases [H₂] and [I₂] until Q = 50.
A student who thinks K adjusts to the concentrations picks this. At temperature T, K is fixed at 50; it is the concentrations, and hence Q, that change until Q = K.
questions.explain: Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 0.20²/(0.20 × 0.20) = 1.0. Q < K, so the ratio of product to reactant terms is too small: net forward reaction increases [HI] and decreases [H₂] and [I₂] until Q = 50.
questions.working: Q = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = (0.20)²/(0.20 × 0.20) = 1.0. Q (1.0) < K (50), so net forward reaction occurs.

questions.q:
N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)   K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ at a certain high temperature
A sealed vessel at this temperature initially contains N₂ at 0.80 mol dm⁻³ and O₂ at 0.20 mol dm⁻³, and no NO. What is the concentration of NO at equilibrium?
options: 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³
8.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³
1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
3.2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the power on [NO] gets [NO] = K[N₂][O₂] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³. The coefficient 2 makes the term [NO]², so a square root is needed: [NO] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.
A student who writes 2[NO] instead of [NO]² gets 2[NO] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, so [NO] = 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³. The coefficient is a power: [NO]² = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, [NO] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

Because K is very small, very little N₂ and O₂ react, so [N₂]eqm ≈ 0.80 and [O₂]eqm ≈ 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Then [NO]² = K[N₂][O₂] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.80 × 0.20 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, so [NO] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Only 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ of each reactant is used, which confirms the approximation.
A student who adds the reactant concentrations gets [NO]² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × (0.80 + 0.20), so [NO] = 3.2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. The terms are multiplied: [NO]² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.80 × 0.20.
questions.explain: Because K is very small, very little N₂ and O₂ react, so [N₂]eqm ≈ 0.80 and [O₂]eqm ≈ 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Then [NO]² = K[N₂][O₂] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.80 × 0.20 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶, so [NO] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Only 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ of each reactant is used, which confirms the approximation.
questions.working: K = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]). K is very small, so the amounts of N₂ and O₂ that react are negligible: [N₂]eqm ≈ 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [O₂]eqm ≈ 0.20 mol dm⁻³. [NO]² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.80 × 0.20 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶; [NO] = √(1.6 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.26 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Check: N₂ used = [NO]/2 = 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, less than 0.1% of 0.80 and about 0.3% of 0.20 mol dm⁻³, so the approximation is valid.

questions.q:
For a reaction at 298 K, ΔG⦵ = +5.70 kJ mol⁻¹.
Which statement about the position of equilibrium for this reaction at 298 K is correct?
options: K is less than 1, so reactants predominate at equilibrium.
K is greater than 1, so products predominate at equilibrium.
No products are present, as a positive ΔG⦵ prevents reaction.
Equilibrium is reached slowly, because ΔG⦵ is positive.
optionWhy: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, so a positive ΔG⦵ means ln K is negative and K < 1: K = e^(−5700/(8.31 × 298)) = 0.100. The position of equilibrium lies to the left, but some products are present.
A student who drops the minus sign from ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K picks this. With the minus sign, a positive ΔG⦵ gives a negative ln K, so K = 0.100, which is less than 1.
A student who reads a positive ΔG⦵ as 'no reaction at all' picks this. K = e^(−ΔG⦵/RT) = 0.100 is small but not zero, so the equilibrium mixture contains some products.
A student who links the position of equilibrium with rate picks this. ΔG⦵ and K describe how far the reaction goes at equilibrium, not how fast equilibrium is reached.
questions.explain: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, so a positive ΔG⦵ means ln K is negative and K < 1: K = e^(−5700/(8.31 × 298)) = 0.100. The position of equilibrium lies to the left, but some products are present.
